title: Usamah ibn Zayd
hookLine: appointed a general at around eighteen, over senior men

cards: The name of the new commander goes around the camp in Medina. Older men hear it and frown. They have fought for years.
They were there at the hard beginnings. And the one put in charge of them is young enough to be their son. People start to talk: is this really the right choice?
The talk reaches the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and he stands up to answer it. Today: the son of yesterday's Zayd.

teach.b: Usamah was the son of Zayd ibn Harithah, and tradition remembers him as very young when he was given command. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps what happened when the grumbling started.
Abdullah ibn Umar reports that the Prophet sent out an army and made Usamah its leader, and some people found fault with his leadership. So the Prophet answered them.

teach.h: SOME FOUND FAULT WITH HIS LEADERSHIP.
teach.b: If you find fault with his leadership, he said, you found fault with his father's leadership before him.

By God, his father was fit to lead, and he was among the people dearest to me, and this son is among the people dearest to me after him. Notice what the answer does. It doesn't say: he's young, but give him a chance.
It ties Usamah to his father, a freed man who had also been doubted, and says both were fit. The objection is treated as an old habit showing up again, not as wisdom.

teach.h: FIT TO LEAD, AND DEAR TO ME.
teach.b: And it puts love on the record, out loud, in front of the men who were complaining.
Tradition adds that the army had not yet left when the Prophet died, and that Abu Bakr, soon after, sent it out under Usamah anyway, as it had been planned.
The tradition gives him a nickname: the beloved, son of the beloved.
Young, and trusted. The trust did not wait for him to get older. It was given first, and then it was defended.

how: Muslims tell the story of Usamah ibn Zayd's command from Sahih al-Bukhari, where the Prophet answers those who doubted the young leader by pointing to his father.

o: Zayd's young son, made commander of an army
Abu Bakr's son, who carried his father's banner
an old companion who led the army at Badr

games.q: Usamah ibn Zayd — tap the pairs.
p: his father, also doubted as a leader
sent the army out after the Prophet died

s: no one objected to Usamah's command
Bukhari says some people found fault with his leadership.
the Prophet answered by pointing to Usamah's father
you found fault with his father's leadership before him, and he was fit to lead.
the Prophet said Usamah should wait until he was older
he defended him as fit to lead, and called him dear to him.

games.q: you are the Prophet. older men are grumbling that the commander you chose is too young. what do you do?
o: replace him with an older man.
defend him in public, and name his father.
say nothing and let him prove himself.
games.why: Bukhari reports he answered them openly: you doubted his father too, both were fit to lead, and both are dear to me.

practice: Bring to mind someone younger than you, a child, a student, a new colleague, and one thing they could do that you usually do yourself or check twice; picture handing it over, and notice anything that resists.
Then think how you'd speak up for them if someone doubted them. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom for the young people around you.

wordCard.voice: Usamah, the young son of a freed man, given command over older companions, and defended by the Prophet as fit to lead. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name Usamah, son of Zayd.

carryVoice: Your line: young and trusted. Age wasn't the measure; being fit to lead was. See you tomorrow.
